questions.model_answer: a) Metronidazole: concentration-dependent killing; PAE present. b) Clindamycin: time-dependent killing; PAE present. c) Vancomycin: time-dependent (AUC/MIC-driven); modest PAE present. d) Fluoroquinolones: concentration-dependent (peak/MIC and AUC/MIC); PAE present against GNB. e) Aminoglycosides: concentration-dependent; PAE present against GNB (2-6 h). f) Imipenem: time-dependent (T>MIC); unlike other beta-lactams it does produce a PAE against GNB.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the aminoglycoside entry is grounded in this chapter (Mandell 9e ch.25, concentration-dependent killing and PAE, pp. 309-310); the other agents rest on standard PK/PD teaching (Craig, IDSA).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort marks metronidazole and imipenem as having no PAE; standard PK/PD data (and this chapter noting imipenem as the beta-lactam exception) credit both with a PAE against their target organisms.

questions.model_answer: a) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems lower antiepileptic levels). b) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency). c) Doxycycline over Septra/TMP-SMX (not used to treat CDI and low risk of inducing CDI). d) Fluconazole over caspofungin (superior renal/urinary penetration; echinocandins negligible in urine). e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir (superior anti-CMV activity). f) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (for bacteria in the CNS).

cohort_answer.text: a) Pip/Tazo over Mero because patient on tegretol. b) Atovaquone over Dapsone because patient has G6PD deficiency. c) Doxycycline over Septra because drug not used for CDI treatment and not associated with development of CDI. d) Fluconazole over Caspofungin because it has superior renal penetration. e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir because it works better for CMV. f) Moxifloxacin over Levofloxacin because it works better for a bacteria in the CNS.

questions.question: A patient has an odontogenic infection.

parts.text: Name two bugs not covered by amoxicillin.
Name two bugs not covered by metronidazole.
Explain why metronidazole covers anaerobes and not aerobes.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 bugs not covered by amox
Name 2 bugs not covered by metronidazole
Explain why metronidazole only covers anaerobe and not aerobe

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). b) Aerobes/facultatives, which lie outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. c) Metronidazole must be reductively activated by low-redox electron carriers (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobes; the reduced nitro radical breaks bacterial DNA strands. Aerobes lack these carriers and oxygen re-oxidizes the intermediate, so the drug is never activated.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not given in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Bugs not covered by amox: Fusobacterium (some resistance to PCN, significant resistance to clindamycin and linezolid; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos and carbapenems); Prevotella (significant resistance to clindamycin; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid); Porphyromonas (susceptible to Flagyl and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid; significant resistance to clindamycin); Peptostreptococcus. Bugs not covered by metronidazole: all the aerobes - Streptococcus, Moraxella, Lactobacillus, Enterobacteriaceae. Why metronidazole only covers anaerobes: the enzyme that activates/oxidizes metronidazole (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase / ferredoxin) is only present in anaerobic bacteria, not aerobic ones.

questions.model_answer: a) Aerobic/facultative organisms outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. b) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). c) Metronidazole requires reductive activation by low-redox electron-transport proteins (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobic bacteria; once reduced, the nitro radical fragments DNA. Aerobes lack this reductive machinery and ambient oxygen re-oxidizes any activated drug, so it is never converted to its cytotoxic form.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not stated in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Actinomyces; Propionibacterium acnes; Lactobacillus. b) H. flu (beta lactamase); Moraxella (beta lactamase); B. fragilis; Prevotella. c) Reductive activation only occurs in obligate anaerobes; reductive particles (nitrogen radicals) interact with DNA causing strand breakage and fatal destabilization of DNA helix.
